Am Mittwoch, 26. September 2018 22:24:08 UTC+2 schrieb Christen Fleming:
> Hi Ines,
>
> 2) e-obs and ARGOS data should be automatically calibrated during as.telemetry(). The trend I found with Scott's calibration data was that e-obs devices that were missing many fixes had a much smaller UERE.
>
> 4.1) The second (higher resolution?) variogram plot looks possibly okay to me. For your analysis, you just want the first few lags to match (up to how large of gaps you will simulate through). If the sampling is irregular, you might consider bumping up the res argument until the variogram stops changing, or using fast=FALSE. This decreases some of the distortion from irregular sampling, but its not possible to remove all of it.  Remaining distortion you can examine by simulating tracks under the same irregular sampling schedule and looking at their resulting variograms.
>
> 4.2) How much IID data your autocorrelated data is worth for estimating the mean, the home-range area, and the RMS speed.
>
> 4.3) I recommend doing everything manually like you have for the first animal, and then automating (interactive=FALSE in ctmm.guess) everything in a way that saves the comparison plots to look over at the end. For 25 animals, I don't think 25 plots would be terrible to look at.
>

> > >

> > >

messages.subject: high hdop points and uere
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
Newbie here, but I am working on estimating home ranges from some archival GPS tags using ctmm.  The tags report hdop values for each point.  I also did a calibration with each tag (15 points in a fixed location) to generate a uere estimate.
My question is if I should still utilize an hdop cutoff for including points (<5, based on manufacturer recommendation), or if having the uere estimate in the telemetry data will minimize their impact on the home range estimate, and therefore I should include all of the points taken.
Some of the high hdop points make biological sense, and am dealing with some small sample sizes, so would hate to exclude meaningful data.
Thanks!
Chris

The great thing about calibrating your data and feeding that into error-informed analyses is that you get to keep all of your data... except the outliers, which you can examine with the outlie() function.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: high hdop points and uere
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I think the R function you want is which(). Let's say you wanted to filter out speed estimates above 5 meters/second. That would look like this:

OUT <- outlie(RAW)
BADDIE <- which(OUT$speed>5) # these are the indices you want
CLEAN <- RAW[-BADDIE,]

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Barriers within home ranges
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I am analyzing home ranges in bison from multiple conservation herds (I believe we met at TWS in Cleveland a few weeks ago). Many of these herds are restricted by linear barriers such as fences or bodies of water. I was wondering if/how ctmm accounts for these features in akde calculations?

Thanks,

Rob
messages.body_snippet:
Hi Chris,

I am analyzing home ranges in bison from multiple conservation herds (I believe we met at TWS in Cleveland a few weeks ago). Many of these herds are restricted by linear barriers such as fe

messages.subject: Re: Barriers within home ranges
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob,

Nice to hear from you.

KDE methods, in general, spill over boundaries by an amount proportional to the bandwidth, which means that they are still asymptotically consistent but have positive bias in the unavailable area.

The rigorous solution is to develop covariate-informed movement models that respect boundaries and then, in AKDE, use boundary-respecting kernels generated by the diffusion process of those models. This is at least a couple of years out, but is a long-term goal.

The simple and immediate solution is to lop off the density estimate at the boundary. We did some simulation tests in our upcoming Ecological Monographs paper and I was surprised at how well this method works. The easiest way to do this is in the CDF slot of the UD object. This is a matrix with row-column indices corresponding to the x & y coordinates stored in the r slot of the UD object. If a location (x[i],y[j]) lies across a boundary, then you set CDF[i,j]=1, which pushes that area outside of the 100% coverage area. The area estimates output by summary() are calculated from the CDF. This is also the default plotted estimate.

Alternatively, with the PDF slot, if that's what you want to work with because you want to average the densities or something, you can set PDF[i,j]=0 for all unavailable (x[i],y[j]), which sets the density to zero there, and then renormalize according to PDF=PDF/(sum(PDF)*prod(dr)), where the dr slot of the UD object contains the grid spacing information for integration.

These two procedures are not exactly equivalent, however, so if you need both the CDF & PDF and need them to be exactly consistent, then there are further steps generate one from the other.

Best,
Chris
